# Incident Report: IcedID Infection on DESKTOP-KKITB6Q

## Evidence reviewed
- `2021-09-10-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (only artifact in the evidence directory; no separate IDS/Suricata alert export was provided)

## Victim host
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 | 10.9.10.102 |
| MAC | 00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3 |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-KKITB6Q (FQDN `desktop-kkitb6q.angrypoutine.com`) |
| Logged-in user | `hobart.gunnarsson` |
| AD domain / DC | `angrypoutine.com`, DC `ANGRYPOUTINE-DC` at 10.9.10.9 |

Grounding: DHCP request (frame at t=0) ties MAC `00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3` to hostname `DESKTOP-KKITB6Q`; ARP confirms that MAC owns 10.9.10.102; Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ exchanges between 10.9.10.102 and the DC (10.9.10.9) carry `CNameString = hobart.gunnarsson` and realm `ANGRYPOUTINE.COM`, with an explicit SPN reference to `host,desktop-kkitb6q.angrypoutine.com`. NBNS/Browser protocol frames from 10.9.10.102 also announce `DESKTOP-KKITB6Q`.

## Malware family
**IcedID (Bokbot)** — attribution is **behavioral**, not signature-confirmed (no IDS/alert artifact was supplied with this evidence).

Basis for the call:
1. At t=139.2s the host resolves `simpsonsavingss.com` -> 194.62.42.206, then immediately issues `GET /bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/MLdmpfjaX/5uFG3Dz7yt/date1?BNLv65=pAAS` with a spoofed legacy User-Agent (`Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; ...)`). This is the classic IcedID "gate" pattern: a nested, randomized alphanumeric URI path terminating in a `dateN`-style filename.
2. The server response is `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="date6"`, delivering a **PE32+ DLL** (MZ/PE header confirmed), not a document or image — a disguised loader/bot module.
3. Within ~4 seconds of that download, the host opens a TCP/443 session to 167.172.37.9 and, shortly after, begins a long sequence of repeated TCP/443 sessions to 94.158.245.52 that continue for the remainder of the capture (~74 minutes, dozens of discrete sessions) — a beaconing pattern.
4. Both 167.172.37.9 and 94.158.245.52 present **the same self-signed TLS certificate** with subject/issuer fields `London, London, "LL EST", "UK System", londonareloeli.uk` and no SNI extension sent by the client — i.e., the malware connects directly to a bare IP over TLS rather than a legitimate hostname. Identical gibberish self-signed certs served from otherwise unrelated hosting IPs is a well-known C2 fingerprint for this loader family.

This combination (MSIE7 UA gate -> disguised DLL payload -> immediate TLS beaconing on 443 to bare IPs with a shared self-signed cert) is consistent with IcedID/Bokbot; no static or dynamic analysis of the DLL itself was performed, so the identification should be treated as behavioral rather than confirmed by signature or sandbox detonation.

Lateral-movement check: the only SMB/NetServerEnum2 activity observed between 10.9.10.102 and the other local host (10.9.10.103, `DESKTOP-MUYEYV7`) is normal Windows network-browser election traffic (Get Backup List / NetServerEnum2), and SMB traffic to the DC is routine Group Policy (SYSVOL) retrieval. No evidence of lateral movement, credential dumping, or additional payload staging was found in this capture.

## Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | 167.172.37.9:443 | TCP/TLS session immediately following DLL download; self-signed cert `londonareloeli.uk` |
| C2 endpoint | 94.158.245.52:443 | Repeated TCP/TLS beacon sessions (~30+ over 4427s); same self-signed cert `londonareloeli.uk` |
| Domain | simpsonsavingss.com | DNS query at t=139.2s resolving to 194.62.42.206; hosted the payload-delivery HTTP GET |
| URL | http://simpsonsavingss.com/bmdff/BhoHsCtZ/MLdmpfjaX/5uFG3Dz7yt/date1?BNLv65=pAAS | Full HTTP request/response captured on tcp.stream 50 (10.9.10.102:58131 -> 194.62.42.206:80) |
| File (transferred) | `date1` (URI) / `date6` (Content-Disposition filename) | Delivered in the HTTP 200 response on tcp.stream 50 |
| File hash (SHA256) | eed363fc4af7a9070d69340592dcab7c78db4f90710357de29e3b624aa957cf8 | Exported via `tshark --export-objects http`; file type confirmed PE32+ DLL, x86-64 |
| TLS cert identity (context, not a domain lookup) | CN/O fields "UK System" / "londonareloeli.uk" | x509 certificate fields observed identically on both C2 IPs |

## Benign context (not IOCs)
- Windows Update/Defender traffic: `download.windowsupdate.com`, `au.download.windowsupdate.com`, `ctldl.windowsupdate.com` (23.1.237.x, Akamai/Microsoft) delivering `.cab` definition updates and the signed `am_delta_patch_1.349.439.0...exe` Defender antimalware update.
- Microsoft telemetry/services: `*.msedge.net`, `*.footprintdns.com`, `login.live.com`, `officeapps.live.com`, `www.bing.com`, `api.msn.com`, `settings-win.data.microsoft.com`, `v10.events.data.microsoft.com`, `client.wns.windows.com`.
- Microsoft Store thumbnail images from `store-images.s-microsoft.com` (PNG/JPEG objects).
- Local AD/domain traffic: Kerberos, LDAP/CLDAP, DCE/RPC (SAMR, DRSUAPI, LSARPC, Netlogon) between 10.9.10.102 and the DC (10.9.10.9), and SMB/GPO retrieval — all normal domain-joined workstation behavior.
- NBNS/Browser-election broadcast chatter with 10.9.10.103 (`DESKTOP-MUYEYV7`) — normal Windows network browsing, no file transfer or credential material observed.
- SSDP M-SEARCH multicast and `www.msftncsi.com` NCSI connectivity check — OS background noise.
- `myexternalip.com` (34.117.59.81, one TLS session) — could not be tied to the confirmed C2 activity or payload; listed as ambiguous background traffic rather than a malicious indicator.

## Incident summary
The Windows workstation DESKTOP-KKITB6Q (10.9.10.102, MAC 00:4f:49:b1:e8:c3), logged in as domain user `hobart.gunnarsson` on the `angrypoutine.com` domain, retrieved a disguised PE32+ DLL from `simpsonsavingss.com` (194.62.42.206) via a gate-style URL using a spoofed IE7 user agent. Seconds after the download, the host began sustained encrypted C2 beaconing over TCP/443 to 167.172.37.9 and 94.158.245.52, both presenting an identical self-signed TLS certificate ("UK System" / `londonareloeli.uk`). The delivery pattern, disguised DLL payload, and shared self-signed C2 certificate are consistent with an IcedID (Bokbot) infection; this attribution is behavioral, as no IDS alert data was available to confirm it by signature.
